analysis.one_liner: Gives the FDA power to order recalls of unsafe food, drugs, devices, and cosmetics and to fine violators.
analysis.headline: The House Energy and Commerce Committee approved the bill 27-16 and reported it in October 1992, but it never received a House floor vote before that Congress ended on January 3, 1993.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would give the Health and Human Services Secretary authority to order companies to stop distributing and recall any food, drug, or cosmetic that poses a serious risk of injury or death, and let federal courts order recalls of foods, drugs, devices, and cosmetics too [S2, S3]. It would let FDA inspectors temporarily detain suspect products for up to 30 days, take samples, copy records, and photograph conditions during inspections [S3]. It would give the FDA Commissioner subpoena power and allow civil money penalties of up to $1 million per violation for companies ($5 million cap per proceeding) for violations, false statements, bribery of FDA employees, and obstructing investigations [S2, S4]. It would also tighten control over imports, including bonds worth at least triple an article's invoice value and destruction of refused articles that pose serious health risks [S2].
analysis.who_benefits: Everyone who eats food, takes medicines, uses medical devices, or buys cosmetics. Consumers would gain faster removal of dangerous products through mandatory recalls instead of relying on voluntary company recalls, stronger penalties for firms that hide problems or bribe inspectors, and tighter screening of imported products.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Consumers of food, drugs, devices, cosmetics

how_it_helps.text: The Secretary would be required to order companies to cease distribution and recall a food, drug, or cosmetic when there is a reasonable probability it will cause serious adverse health consequences or death, with notice to people exposed to the risk [S2].

FDA would gain power to temporarily detain suspect products (previously limited mainly to devices), collect and retain samples, copy records, and document violations photographically during inspections [S2, S3].

The FDA Commissioner could subpoena witnesses and documents in enforcement investigations, and companies could face civil penalties of up to $250,000 for individuals or $1,000,000 per violation for other persons for violations, false statements, bribery of agency employees, destruction of evidence, or obstruction of investigations [S2, S4].

Imported products that violate the law could be refused entry more broadly, importers would have to post bonds of at least three times invoice value, refused articles would have to be marked before export, and dangerous articles could be destroyed at the owner's expense [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Manufacturers, importers, and distributors of FDA-regulated products, who would face mandatory recall orders, detention of goods, expanded inspections and four-year recordkeeping requirements, subpoenas, civil fines up to $1 million per violation, and stricter import rules including triple-value bonds and destruction of refused goods at their own expense [S2, S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: FDA-regulated food, drug, device, cosmetic firms

drawbacks.text: Mandatory recall orders, 30-day detentions, and broadened inspections would impose compliance and distribution costs on regulated companies, costs that could be passed on in prices; the committee-reported version stays a recall order for only 24 hours or until a court rules on a stay, which gives companies limited time to contest an order [S3].

The bill bars criminal prosecution of a violation if a civil penalty has been assessed, which means a large company could resolve serious violations by paying fines rather than facing criminal charges [S3].
All manufacturers, importers, and distributors would have to keep records for four years and file reports as the Secretary requires, a burden that falls hardest on smaller firms [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is faster removal of dangerous products versus higher compliance costs for regulated companies. The mandatory recall and penalty provisions address a real gap: FDA could not compel a recall of unsafe food, drugs, or cosmetics under then-current law. The costs are real but standard for product-safety enforcement, though the bar on criminal prosecution when a civil penalty is paid and the short window to contest a recall order are legitimate design concerns.

outcome.mechanism: The committee approved and reported the bill to the House floor calendar in October 1992, but no one ever brought it up for a vote before the 102nd Congress ended in January 1993.

narrative.text: Rep. Henry Waxman, joined by Rep. John Dingell, introduced the bill on October 24, 1991, and it was referred to the Energy and Commerce Committee [S1, S4, S6].

The committee held a markup session on July 9, 1992, and ordered the bill reported as amended by a vote of 27 to 16; it was formally reported on October 5, 1992, and placed on the Union Calendar, which is the House floor calendar for bills reported from committee [S6].
No floor vote ever followed; the bill sat on the calendar until the 102nd Congress ended on January 3, 1993, and the Senate never considered a companion [S1, S6].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: FDA-regulated food, drug, device, and cosmetics manufacturers and importers were better off, because they avoided mandatory recall orders, civil fines of up to $1 million per violation, subpoena power, and expanded inspections and recordkeeping. Consumers continued to depend on voluntary recalls of unsafe products.

sides.party_line_note: The record shows the committee vote was 27-16 but does not give the party breakdown of the vote; all named sponsors were Democrats, so the partisan shape of the opposition cannot be confirmed from the provided sources.

industries.note: Drug makers would face mandatory recall orders, subpoena power aimed at them, and civil penalties of up to $1 million per violation for violations, false statements, bribery of agency staff, or destroying evidence [S2, S4]. Their interest in weaker enforcement ran against consumers' interest in getting unsafe drugs off shelves quickly.

For the first time the Secretary could order a mandatory recall of unsafe food, and inspectors could detain suspect food for up to 30 days, take samples, and copy records [S2, S3]. Companies would bear the cost of recalls and destroyed goods.

Courts could order recalls of unsafe devices, seizure authority would cover any device violating the law rather than only adulterated or misbranded ones, and certain device penalty provisions would be replaced [S2, S3].
Cosmetics would be brought under recall orders, detention, inspections, and recordkeeping requirements that previously applied mainly to food, drugs, and devices [S2, S3].

Importers would post bonds of at least triple invoice value, mark refused goods before export, pay for destruction of dangerous refused articles, and face liens on future imports if they defaulted [S2].
